meta.tagline: Chaotic, noisy, full of life — the city that serves the world's best pizza for the least money, wrapped in paper, eaten standing up

pills: The metro has become an art gallery

overview.intro: Naples frightens you first, then won't let you go. Traffic with no rules, narrow streets, noisy crowds. But at the same time Italy's purest cuisine, the world's best pizza, Europe's most densely layered archaeological memory and the incomparable view of the Bay are all here. Vesuvius could wake at any moment — and Naples knows this. That's why the city holds tight to today: loudly, fast and with its whole heart. Stand in the middle of Spaccanapoli and the city pulls you in every direction. Let it.

local_word.definition: Naples' espresso. Italy's strongest, smallest, cheapest coffee. At the counter, in one sip, €1-1.50. The caffè sospeso tradition comes from here too: when someone has a coffee they leave one paid for someone who can't afford it — it stays recorded at the till. You can ask 'is there a sospeso?' Naples invented coffee as a form of sharing.

rules.title: Crowds and noise are normal — don't try to protect yourself from them
rules.description: Naples looks disorganised because it is. Cars run red lights, scooters mount pavements however narrow they are, the concept of a queue exists in shops but isn't observed. No need to panic — the city functions within this chaos. Just be a little more careful, check your pockets and get into the city's rhythm.

rules.title: Pizza is nowhere else this good — and they know it
rules.description: Neapolitan pizza is on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Why it isn't the same elsewhere: Campania's San Marzano tomatoes, mozzarella di bufala, a wood-fired oven at 485°C and dough rested for at least 8 hours. Margherita or Marinara — that's all. No extra sauces, no toppings, no fillings. The skill is in the simplicity; adding extras is the mistake.

rules.title: Half a day isn't enough for Pompeii — plan a full day
rules.description: Pompeii is 30-40 minutes from Naples and most people grasp its real scale only when they're there: 66 hectares, 11,000 inhabitants, forum, theatre, baths, villas. Seeing it in half a day is possible but stays superficial. It opens at 9am and is most crowded at midday — getting in at opening is the best approach. Herculaneum is much smaller but far better preserved; if you're seeing both, go to Herculaneum first.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Alibus to Piazza Garibaldi or Piazza Municipio · €5

quick_facts.label: Metro
quick_facts.sub: Single fare €1.50 · 90 minutes valid · funicular included

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.sub: Apr–May and Sep–Oct ideal · Jun–Aug very hot · Dec–Feb mild

quick_facts.label: Pizza
quick_facts.sub: L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele · €5–8 · bring cash

tip.label: Carry cash — cards aren't accepted everywhere
tip.text: Naples' small pizzerias, street stalls, bars and some trattorias want cash. ATMs are widespread across the city but scarce in some smaller neighbourhoods. Carrying €50-100 cash daily makes things easier. In smaller places in Quartieri Spagnoli and Spaccanapoli particularly, there may be no card machine.

overview.title: Welcome to Naples

transport.intro: The metro has become an art gallery, funiculars climb the hills, buses are chaotic but they work. Walking is the best option for the centre.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: The Alibus (ANM) goes from the airport to Piazza Garibaldi (Naples Centrale train station) and Piazza Municipio. Ticket €5, departures every 15-20 minutes. Fixed-price taxi to the city centre: €25-35. Alibus is the most practical option — cheaper than a taxi. There's no direct metro connection from the airport; Alibus drops you at Piazza Garibaldi where you can connect to the metro.

items.title: Line 1 — Art Metro
items.description: One of Naples' most special experiences: Toledo, Università, Garibaldi and Municipio stations were designed by international artists. Toledo station was voted Europe's most beautiful metro station in 2012. Single fare €1.50, valid 90 minutes, funiculars included. Runs the full length of the historic centre.

items.title: Funiculars — the climb to Vomero
items.description: Four funicular lines climb Naples' hills: Funicolare Centrale from Piazzetta Augusteo to Vomero; Funicolare di Chiaia from Via del Parco Margherita to Vomero; Funicolare di Montesanto from Piazza Montesanto to San Martino; Funicolare di Mergellina from the Mergellina waterfront to the Posillipo hilltop. Same ticket system, €1.50.

items.title: Bus — chaotic but comprehensive
items.description: City buses run on the same ticket system. Necessary for reaching neighbourhoods the metro and funiculars can't access. Can run late during busy hours. Buy tickets in advance — not available on the bus. Available at stops or tabacchi shops.

items.title: Walking — and caution
items.description: Spaccanapoli, Via dei Tribunali, Quartieri Spagnoli and the historic centre are all walkable. Pavements are narrow, scooters come from every direction — be careful. Safe to walk at night but avoid isolated streets and don't carry valuables visibly. The centre isn't large: 15 minutes from Piazza del Gesù to Toledo.

callout.label: Campania ArteCard — museums and transport combined
callout.text: The 3-day Naples ArteCard (€21) covers all city public transport (metro, bus, funicular) and gives free entry to the first two museums, discounted entry to others. Includes the Naples National Museum, Certosa di San Martino and Capodimonte. Worth considering if you're planning a museum-heavy itinerary. The 3-day card covering all of Campania is €32 — Pompeii and Herculaneum included.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Naples' neighbourhoods are very different from each other. The historic centre is close to everything, Vomero is quiet and panoramic, Chiaia is modern and on the waterfront.

local_word.definition: The street that splits Naples down the middle — its name says exactly that: 'Naples splitter'. It's actually a series of connected streets; Via Benedetto Croce and Via San Biagio dei Librai are the most important sections. This route dating from Roman times is full of cathedrals, churches, shops, bars and life. Walking it is the shortest way to understand the city.

items.name: Centro Storico — historic centre
items.description: Spaccanapoli, Via dei Tribunali, San Gregorio Armeno (the Christmas figurine street) are all in this neighbourhood. The neighbourhood itself, Naples' historic centre (Centro Storico), has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. Walking distance to everything but busy and noisy. Nightlife is lively, early morning is the quietest. Budget hotels and small family guesthouses (B&B) are most plentiful in this area.

items.name: Quartieri Spagnoli
items.description: A grid of narrow streets built for Spanish soldiers in the 16th century. Laundry hangs from window to window, children play in the alleyways, a bar on every corner. Diego Maradona's mural portrait is here — on Via Emanuele De Deo. Touristy but still a real neighbourhood. Walking distance to Toledo metro and Via Toledo.

items.name: Chiaia
items.description: Modern neighbourhood on the Bay waterfront, stretching along the Lungomare. High-quality restaurants, bars and shops. Mergellina harbour is nearby. An evening walk along the Lungomare is one of Naples' most enjoyable activities. Slightly further from the historic centre but easily reached by taxi or metro.

items.name: Vomero
items.description: The hilltop neighbourhood reached by funicular. Castel Sant'Elmo and Certosa di San Martino are here — both among the city's finest viewpoints. Away from the crowds of the historic centre, quieter and more local. Ten minutes to the centre by funicular. Good for morning local cafés and market shopping.

items.name: Near Piazza Garibaldi
items.description: Walking distance to Naples Centrale. The Circumvesuviana train (Pompeii, Herculaneum, Sorrento) departs from here. Practical for day trips. The neighbourhood itself is very touristy but the most central point for transport. Prices are relatively reasonable.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Naples can be visited year-round but summer brings higher temperatures and tourist density.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April and May are Naples' most balanced period. Temperatures around 18-24°C, the Bay at its most vivid, tourists present but away from peak season. Maggio dei Monumenti (May Monuments Month): normally closed historic buildings and private spaces open for visits — follow this programme. Semana Santa (Easter) period brings religious processions and ceremonies through the city.

callout.label: Maggio dei Monumenti — normally closed doors open
callout.text: Every May, Naples City Council opens hundreds of normally closed historic buildings, private collections and hidden courtyards to visitors. Free or symbolically priced. Palaces, underground churches, private gardens. The programme changes every year; follow napolicultura.it. The best reason to visit Naples in May.

items.subtitle: Spring · Mild weather, fewer crowds, festivals

items.label: Summer
items.name: Hot, crowded and lively
items.description: July and August are the busiest and hottest months. The Amalfi Coast and Capri are at their peak — you won't get in without reservations. But Naples itself is something else on summer evenings: aperitivo on the Lungomare, fish restaurants in Posillipo, gelato in Mergellina. The city is at its most alive and bearable before 10am and after 8pm.

callout.label: Posillipo — the city's finest evening
callout.text: The hilltop neighbourhood west of Chiaia, looking out over the Bay. The view of Vesuvius and the Bay from Posillipo's restaurants and bars in the late afternoon is exceptional. Take a bus or taxi from Mergellina. As the sun sets the colour of the Bay changes — be there at sunset to catch this view.

items.subtitle: Summer · Above 35°C, Bay beautiful, nightlife peaks

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October see the crowds thin while the weather stays mild. The sea is still warm enough to swim. The Amalfi Coast and Capri are much more comfortable to visit. Trattorias open with new seasonal menus — walnut pasta, courgette flowers, fresh fish. Rain increases in November but museums and historic sites are nearly empty.

callout.label: Amalfi Coast — autumn's finest escape
callout.text: From Naples, SITA buses or ferries can take you to Amalfi, Positano and Ravello. In September-October, away from summer crowds, prices lower, the scenery unchanged. Check the ferry season from Positano back to Naples — some services end in late October.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Summer crowds gone, sea still warm

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and affordable
items.description: December Christmas preparations bring the city to life — San Gregorio Armeno's Christmas figurine street is at its peak this time of year. January and February are Naples' quietest period. Museums nearly empty, no queues at Pompeii, hotels cheap. Temperatures 10-15°C, some rainy days. During Carnevale (February), struffoli and sfogliatella are in season at pastry shops.

callout.label: San Gregorio Armeno — the Christmas figurine street
callout.text: In the Centro Storico, between Via dei Tribunali and Spaccanapoli. Handmade nativity scene figures (presepe) are sold here year-round but in December the street comes fully alive. Alongside traditional figures, satirical likenesses of famous people are also made — politicians, footballers, the year's talking points. Walking through is free; go into the corner workshops and watch the craftspeople at work.

items.subtitle: Winter · Least crowded, best prices

monthly_highlights.text: The miracle of San Gennaro: the city waits for the saint's blood to liquefy in the Duomo; if it does, Naples celebrates — the city's most charged day.
San Gregorio Armeno: the street of presepe (nativity) workshops becomes a human river before Christmas; the figurines include politicians and footballers.
Pizza Village: a giant pizza festival on the lungomare — hundreds of ovens, concerts, Guinness attempts.
Pastiera season: the orange-blossom wheat tart never leaves the bakeries; with casatiello bread, it is the taste of a Naples spring.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: The Neapolitan pizza that entered UNESCO's list in 2017 — when King Umberto I and Queen Margherita visited Naples in 1889, pizzaiolo Raffaele Esposito prepared a pizza carrying the colours of the Italian flag: red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil. The pizza named after the Queen is known everywhere in the world today, but its real taste is still only here. Naples doesn't stop there: sfogliatella, cuoppo, pizza fritta — this city eats on the street, at the counter, standing up.

local_word.definition: Wallet pizza. A small margherita, baked in 90 seconds, folded four times straight from the oven, wrapped in paper, hot and carried in hand. €2. Sold at many places along Via dei Tribunali. Be careful on the first bite — the melted cheese and tomato sauce inside can be dangerously hot. Wait a minute.

items.name: Neapolitan pizza — the real thing
items.description: Margherita (San Marzano tomatoes, mozzarella di bufala, basil) or Marinara (tomatoes, garlic, oregano — no cheese). No other options, no other options needed. L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele at Via Cesare Sersale 1 — since 1870, only these two varieties, cash payment, long queue. Sorbillo on Via dei Tribunali — shorter queue, same quality. Order another before you're halfway through the first.

items.name: Pizza fritta
items.description: During World War II Naples was bombed, the wood-fired ovens were destroyed but frying oil was still available — so pizza began to be cooked in hot oil rather than an oven. Pizza fritta was born from these difficulties. The dough is filled with ricotta, cicoli (fried pork skin) and provola cheese and puffs up in hot oil. Sophia Loren fried this pizza in a famous film scene. €3-5, a full meal on its own. The pizzeria called 1947 Pizza Fritta is at Via Pietro Colletta 29-31.

items.name: Sfogliatella
items.description: A shell-shaped ricotta pastry — layered and crispy outside, filled with cinnamon ricotta and candied fruit inside. Two versions: riccia (crispy layered) and frolla (covered in short pastry on the outside, softer). The fresh version comes out of the oven in the early morning hours. La Sfogliatella Mary is inside Galleria Umberto I. An espresso alongside — this is the authentic Neapolitan morning.
items.tag: La Sfogliatella Mary, Galleria Umberto I · fresh in the morning · €1.50–2

items.name: Cuoppo
items.description: Mixed fried food in a paper cone: the seafood version (cuoppo di mare) has prawns, squid, mussels; the land version (cuoppo di terra) has courgette flowers, aubergine, potato chips. Around Pignasecca Market or Piazza Monteoliveto. €4-6. Eat while walking — no seating.
items.tag: Around Pignasecca Market · €4–6 · eat while walking

items.name: Ragù napoletano
items.description: Pork and tomato sauce cooked for hours — sometimes 5-6 hours — on the lowest heat. Monday and Thursday are the traditional days; your chance of finding it at trattorias is highest on those days. Served with spaghetti, rigatoni or ziti. Crusco bread alongside, the meal is complete. Trattoria da Nennella in Quartieri Spagnoli.
items.tag: Trattoria da Nennella, Quartieri Spagnoli · Mon-Thu · €10–14

items.name: Espresso — and caffè sospeso
items.description: Neapolitan espresso: strong, small and €1-1.50. Drink at the counter, standing, fast — this is Naples coffee culture. The caffè sospeso (suspended coffee) tradition: an extra coffee paid into the till, for someone without means later. To take part, say 'sospeso' and pay for two coffees, leaving one behind. One of Naples' most humane rituals.
items.tag: Any bar · €1–1.50 at the counter · join the sospeso tradition

callout.label: Pignasecca Market — 7am to 1pm
callout.text: Right next to Quartieri Spagnoli, on Via Pignasecca. Naples' most lively open-air food market. Fresh fish, vegetables, fruit, cheese, street food. Open 7am-1pm, closed Sundays. Inside the market: cuoppo stalls, mozzarella sellers and breakfast bars. Not touristy, a genuine neighbourhood market. Prices low, quality high.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Naples' most interesting corners are usually just one street away from the crowds — some in the city's underground, some on its hilltops.

items.name: Toledo Metro Station
items.description: Toledo station on Line 1 won the award for Europe's most beautiful metro station in 2012. Designed by Oscar Tusquets: blue-purple mosaic surfaces that give a cave-like feeling as you descend deeper, themes of sea and light. No extra charge for entry — included in a standard metro ticket. Add Municipio, Università and Garibaldi stations: each is the work of a different artist. This metro line alone is worth making the journey for.
items.rarity: Europe's most beautiful metro station — and an art gallery

items.name: Galleria Borbonica
items.description: On Via Morelli, near Chiaia. Built in the 19th century as an escape tunnel for King Ferdinand II. Later became a hospital, police depot and World War II air raid shelter. Inside, old cars and motorcycles from the 1940s-50s are still there. Different from Napoli Sotterranea: here it's not ancient Rome but recent history. Several different tour options available. Advance reservation essential.
items.rarity: WWII shelter, Bourbon tunnel and abandoned cars

items.name: Castel Sant'Elmo
items.description: A star-shaped castle on the Vomero hilltop, reachable by funicular. Dating from the 14th century. From its terraces: Vesuvius, the Bay, Capri and the whole city visible 360 degrees. The adjacent Certosa di San Martino (former Carthusian monastery) converted to a museum — the city's richest museum in terms of Neapolitan art and history. Both reachable by the same funicular.
items.rarity: Vesuvius and Bay views — the city's finest viewpoint

items.name: Quartieri Spagnoli murals
items.description: Diego Maradona's enormous portrait on Via Emanuele De Deo has been here since 1990 — painted, removed, painted again. Naples, which Maradona led to championships in 1987 and 1990, regards him like a saint; there are statues and shrines to him on the street. Walking through the neighbourhood you see not just Maradona but dozens of other murals: paintings telling of Naples' identity, history and politics. Free, walkable.
items.rarity: Maradona's home and a neighbourhood's memory

items.name: Teatro Greco-Romano di Neapolis
items.description: In Spaccanapoli, on Via Anticaglia. A 2nd-century Roman theatre now buried under buildings. The old arches of the theatre are visible through the narrow streets between them. Literally the traces of a history built over by the city. Some sections can be visited on guided tours; consider combining with Napoli Sotterranea.
items.rarity: An ancient Roman theatre under a house

items.name: Museo di Capodimonte
items.description: In the north of the city, inside Capodimonte Park. Former Bourbon palace, now museum. Caravaggio, Titian, Raphael, Botticelli — and Andy Warhol's famous Vesuvius series. A fraction of the Naples National Museum's visitor numbers. The extensive park is also free to walk through. 30-40 minutes by bus from the city centre but a place where you could spend hours.
items.rarity: Naples' quietest museum — and its most comprehensive collection

callout.label: Lungomare — evening walk and the Bay
callout.text: The coastal road stretching from Castel dell'Ovo to Mergellina. Between 7pm and 9pm Neapolitans walk here, eat ice cream, sit. Views of Vesuvius and the Bay, Capri's silhouette across the water. Free entry, walking distance about 3 kilometres. One of Naples' most beautiful hours — you see the city's finest views without paying for anything.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat pizza at L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele
items.sub: Via Cesare Sersale 1. Only Margherita or Marinara. Bring cash. Be ready for the queue — usually 20-40 minutes.

items.label: Visit Toledo metro station
items.sub: Line 1. Included in a standard metro ticket. Blue-purple mosaics that change as you descend. Also visit Municipio and Università.

items.label: Walk Spaccanapoli end to end
items.sub: Via Benedetto Croce and Via San Biagio dei Librai. Everything from cathedrals to bars is here. Early morning is the quietest.

items.label: Eat sfogliatella — fresh in the morning
items.sub: La Sfogliatella Mary, Galleria Umberto I. Fresh from the oven in the early morning hours. €1.50-2. Order an espresso alongside.

items.label: Try pizza fritta
items.sub: 1947 Pizza Fritta, Via Pietro Colletta 29-31. Fried, filled, light. €3-5. Sophia Loren's pizza.

items.label: Take part in the caffè sospeso ritual
items.sub: Order an espresso at any bar, say 'sospeso' to the till and pay for two coffees. One stays with you, one is for a stranger.

items.label: Go to Pignasecca Market in the morning
items.sub: Via Pignasecca. 7am-1pm. Fresh fish, cuoppo, mozzarella. Closed Sundays.

items.label: Find the Maradona mural in Quartieri Spagnoli
items.sub: Via Emanuele De Deo. Here since 1990. Also explore the other murals around it.

items.label: Take the funicular up to Castel Sant'Elmo
items.sub: Funicolare Centrale or Chiaia. Vomero hilltop. 360° views: Vesuvius, the Bay, Capri. Certosa di San Martino next door.

items.label: Visit Galleria Borbonica
items.sub: Via Morelli, near Chiaia. WWII shelter, old cars. Advance reservation essential.

items.label: Take an evening walk along the Lungomare
items.sub: From Castel dell'Ovo to Mergellina. 7-9pm. Views of Vesuvius. Free.

items.label: Set aside a full day for Pompeii or Herculaneum
items.sub: Circumvesuviana train from Piazza Garibaldi. Pompeii ~35 min, Herculaneum ~20 min. Both open at 9am — arriving at opening is best.

checklist.title: Naples Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Naples will pull you back even harder next time.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Naples looks chaotic, but its rules are clear. Know these four and the city will open itself to you without fear.

items.name: Burying hours in one pizzeria's queue
items.description: Da Michele is legend, but a two-hour tourist queue doesn't make the pizza better; every Naples neighbourhood has its own master.
items.instead: If the queue overflows, walk two streets: Sorbillo, Di Matteo, Starita or a nameless local oven — all in the same league.

items.name: 'Private guide' hunters at Garibaldi and Pompeii
items.description: The 'official guides' who approach at the station and the ruins' gate sell mediocre tours at inflated prices; some tickets turn out fake.
items.instead: Buy Pompeii tickets from the official site; if you want a guide, hire a licensed one inside — never deal on the Circumvesuviana.

items.name: The 'broken meter' taxi
items.description: The 'meter's broken' classic in Naples taxis is the opening move of the tourist tariff.
items.instead: Ask for the meter before boarding or point to the fixed-fare route list; failing that, call an app — and the metro is the city's finest art gallery anyway.

items.name: Street bargains on 'brand-new' phones
items.description: Hand-sold 'sealed' phones and watches are the city's oldest game: a stone in the box, a hole in your pocket.
items.instead: Never buy electronics on the street; for a gift take a corno (the red horn) — cheap, local, and the city swears it brings luck.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Safety in Naples is less about which street than about bearing: wave the phone less, wear the bag across, smile at the chaos. The city is kind to guests; panic is what marks the tourist.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From Spaccanapoli to the Vesuvius view

steps.title: Walk Spaccanapoli
steps.description: Follow the line that splits the city: churches, presepe workshops, life hanging from balconies. Morning coffee standing at Gambrinus.

steps.title: Cappella Sansevero
steps.description: The Veiled Christ's miracle in marble; book ahead, hold your breath inside.

steps.title: Pizza — the real one
steps.description: Margherita or marinara, 90 seconds in a wood oven. Hold it by the crust, fold, eat with gratitude.

steps.title: Toledo metro + Quartieri Spagnoli
steps.description: Surface from Europe's most beautiful metro station and dive into the Spanish Quarter's narrow vertical lanes: murals, the Maradona shrine, the real Naples.

steps.title: Castel Sant'Elmo sunset
steps.description: Take the funicular up to Vomero: from the castle walls, the bay, Vesuvius, and the city simmering below.

steps.title: Chiaia evening
steps.description: Aperitivo in the seaside quarter, then ragù or seafood; close with a sfogliatella.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Centre and view
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Spaccanapoli, Sansevero, pizza, Sant'Elmo.

steps.title: Pompeii day
steps.description: Early Circumvesuviana to Pompeii (give it the full day); a pizza fritta reward at Garibaldi on return. Energy left? Walk the lungomare at night.

steps.title: Underground and hills
steps.description: The tunnels of Napoli Sotterranea or the Galleria Borbonica in the morning, a cuoppo in hand at the port at noon, Capodimonte's Caravaggio in the afternoon, a farewell espresso at night — and leave one sospeso.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Italian opens doors; Neapolitan wins hearts. With these five, the street is yours.

items.meaning: Hi / bye — any hour, to anyone
Please — add it to the end of your order
The Naples greeting — surprise, joy and 'what's up' in one syllable
Neapolitan for 'let's go!' — say jamme jà and the city adopts you
